questions.question_text: A gardening website surveyed customers as they left a plant nursery and reported "**Most households grow their own vegetables** — $76\%$ say yes". What is the main reason the report claims more than the survey shows?

options.text: Everybody surveyed was already shopping at a nursery, so households that garden are over-represented
The survey reports a percentage instead of the number of households that answered
options.why: Objects to the form the figure is written in, which does not change who was surveyed.

options.text: Growing vegetables changes with the season, so the survey should have run all year
options.why: Raises timing, which affects the size of the figure rather than the group it describes.

options.text: The survey should have asked how many vegetables each household grows
options.why: Asks for a different variable when the reported variable was already answered directly.

questions.solution_text:
Every person surveyed had come to a plant nursery, and buying plants is exactly what a household that grows vegetables does.
Households that grow nothing had almost no chance of appearing in the sample.
**Everybody surveyed was already shopping at a nursery, so households that garden are over-represented**.

questions.question_text: A fitness-watch advertisement reads "**Our watch makes you healthier**". The study behind it recorded how many steps each owner logged in the watch’s app over a month. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Steps logged were measured, but health was not, so the claim is unsupported
Steps logged were measured, and more steps means healthier, so the claim is supported
options.why: Treats the measured variable as if it were the claimed one without any measure of health.

options.text: Health was measured indirectly, so the claim is supported for owners of the watch
options.why: Calls an unmeasured quantity indirectly measured, which the study never recorded.

options.text: Neither steps nor health was measured, so the study shows nothing at all
options.why: Dismisses the step count, which the app did record directly and reliably.

questions.solution_text:
The study recorded a step count, which is a number of steps and nothing more.
No measure of health — weight, fitness, blood pressure or anything else — was taken, so no result in the data can rise or fall with health.
**Steps logged were measured, but health was not, so the claim is unsupported**.

questions.question_text: A news report states that children who own more books score higher on reading tests, under the headline "**Buying books raises reading scores**". What is wrong with the headline?

options.text: It states a cause, when the data shows only that the two rise together
It states a cause, when the data shows that higher scores lead to owning more books
options.why: Replaces one unproven causal direction with the opposite one, which the data equally cannot show.

options.text: It reports reading scores, when the study should have reported reading ages
options.why: Objects to the choice of measure rather than to the causal wording of the claim.

options.text: It ignores that children who own no books were left out of the study
options.why: Invents an exclusion the report does not describe, since low book counts are part of the pattern.

questions.solution_text:
The data pairs a book count with a test score for each child and finds that they rise together, which is an association.
An association cannot show which one produced the other, and a household that can afford many books can usually afford other help with reading as well.
**It states a cause, when the data shows only that the two rise together**.

questions.question_text: A snack brand’s packaging states only: "Preferred by most shoppers." Which question should a reader ask **first** to judge the claim?

options.text: How many shoppers were asked, and how were they chosen?
How long has the brand been selling this snack in Australia?
options.why: Asks about the product’s history, which says nothing about how the figure was gathered.

options.text: How much does the snack cost compared with the other brands?
options.why: Asks about price, which is not the variable the preference claim reports.

options.text: Which supermarkets currently stock the snack on their shelves?
options.why: Asks about distribution, which cannot show who was surveyed or how many.

questions.solution_text:
The claim gives no sample size and no description of who was asked, so nothing about it can be checked.
Those two details decide both how much the figure can swing by chance and whether it describes shoppers generally or a group with a reason to prefer the brand.
**How many shoppers were asked, and how were they chosen?**.

questions.question_text: A mining company publishes its own report finding that the river beside its site meets every water-quality standard. How should a reader treat this result?

options.text: Treat it as unconfirmed and look for the same testing done by an independent body
Treat it as false, because a company reporting on itself cannot be believed
options.why: Rejects the finding outright, when funding is a reason to check a study rather than to dismiss it.

options.text: Treat it as settled, because water-quality standards are fixed by regulation
options.why: Assumes fixed standards guarantee honest testing, which is a separate question from the standards.

options.text: Treat it as settled, because the company would face penalties for a false report
options.why: Relies on the threat of penalties instead of checking how and where the samples were taken.

questions.solution_text:
The company gains if the river passes, so it had an interest in where and when the samples were taken and in which results were published.
That interest does not make the finding false, but nothing in the report is checked by anyone without a stake in it.
**Treat it as unconfirmed and look for the same testing done by an independent body**.

questions.question_text: A newspaper puts a "have your say" box on its website asking whether a new tram line should be built, and reports that $64\%$ of the $9000$ respondents said no. Which claim does this figure support?

options.text: Of the readers who chose to respond, $64\%$ opposed the tram line
Of the city’s residents, $64\%$ oppose the tram line
options.why: Extends a figure from self-chosen respondents to a whole city that was never sampled.

options.text: Of the newspaper’s readers, $64\%$ oppose the tram line
options.why: Covers all readers, when only readers who decided to respond are in the figure.

options.text: Of the people living near the route, $64\%$ oppose the tram line
options.why: Names a group whose members were never identified or separated in the responses.

questions.solution_text:
Nobody was selected; each reader decided whether to use the box, and readers who feel strongly about a tram line are the ones who do.
The figure therefore describes exactly the people it collected — those who chose to answer.
**Of the readers who chose to respond, $64\%$ opposed the tram line**.

questions.question_text: A bank emailed a survey to $8000$ customers. It received $320$ replies, of which $88\%$ rated its app easy to use, and headed its press release "$88\%$ of customers find our app easy". Which headline matches the data?

options.text: $88\%$ of the $320$ customers who replied find our app easy
$88\%$ of the $8000$ customers we contacted find our app easy
options.why: Attaches the figure to everyone contacted, when $7680$ of them never answered.

options.text: At least $88\%$ of customers find our app easy
options.why: Turns the figure into a lower bound, when the non-repliers could rate the app far lower.

options.text: $3.5\%$ of our customers find our app easy
options.why: Applies the $88\%$ to the reply rate as though non-repliers had all answered no.

questions.solution_text:
The $88\%$ was calculated from the $320$ replies, which is $4\%$ of the customers contacted.
The $7680$ customers who did not reply left no information about how they would have rated the app.
**$88\%$ of the $320$ customers who replied find our app easy**.

questions.question_text: A study reports that $61\%$ of people aged $18$ to $29$ and $58\%$ of people aged $30$ to $45$ use a bank app every week. The headline reads "**Young adults far more likely to bank by app**". What is the main fault?

options.text: "Far more likely" describes a $3$ percentage point gap between two similar figures
The two age bands cover different numbers of years, so they cannot be compared
options.why: Objects to the band widths, which does not affect the comparison of two percentages.

options.text: The study reports weekly use, when the headline is about likelihood
options.why: Treats weekly use and likelihood of use as different variables, which the headline does not.

options.text: The headline names only one age group, when the study reported two
options.why: Objects to what the headline leaves out rather than to the strength of the word used.

questions.solution_text:
$61\%-58\%=3\%$, so the two groups use a bank app at almost the same rate.
"Far more likely" describes a large gap, and a difference of three percentage points is not one.
**"Far more likely" describes a $3$ percentage point gap between two similar figures**.

questions.question_text: A courier company’s advertisement claims "**Twice as fast as the competition**", comparing its express service with a rival’s cheapest standard service. The rival’s own express service is not mentioned. What is the fault in the comparison?

options.text: The rival is represented by the one service chosen to make the advertiser look best
Delivery speed varies with distance, so no comparison between couriers is possible
options.why: Rules out all comparison, when a like-for-like test over the same routes would work.

options.text: The advertisement gives a ratio instead of the actual delivery times in days
options.why: Objects to the form of the figure rather than to which services were compared.

options.text: Express services cost more, so the comparison should be made on price
options.why: Switches the comparison to a different variable from the one the claim is about.

questions.solution_text:
An express service is designed to be faster than a standard one, so the gap shown comes mostly from comparing two different kinds of service.
The rival’s express service — the one a customer would actually choose against it — is left out.
**The rival is represented by the one service chosen to make the advertiser look best**.

options.text: The overall rise is supported, but "every month" is contradicted by March and May
The claim is fully supported, since June recorded more visitors than January
options.why: Judges a month-by-month claim on the first and last months only, ignoring the falls between.

options.text: The claim is contradicted, since visitor numbers were lower in June than in January
options.why: Misreads the graph: June is the tallest column and January the shortest.

options.text: The claim cannot be judged, since the graph gives no scale on the vertical axis
options.why: Reports a missing scale, when the axis is labelled in thousands from zero.

questions.solution_text:
Visitors fell from $55\,000$ in February to $48\,000$ in March, and again from $61\,000$ in April to $58\,000$ in May.
So two of the five month-to-month steps were falls, even though June ($66\,000$) is well above January ($42\,000$).
**The overall rise is supported, but "every month" is contradicted by March and May**.

questions.question_text: A sports club committee is choosing a uniform supplier. The only evidence it has is a report written by one supplier, stating that "$94\%$ of clubs rate our uniforms highly", with no sample size and no description of which clubs were asked. What should the committee do?

options.text: Ask the supplier how many clubs were asked and how they were chosen before deciding
Accept the $94\%$, since a figure that high leaves plenty of room for error
options.why: Treats a large percentage as its own evidence, when the figure cannot be checked at all.

options.text: Reject the supplier, since a report written by a supplier is always worthless
options.why: Dismisses the report outright, when the missing details could still be supplied and checked.

options.text: Run its own poll of members on which uniform they prefer instead
options.why: Measures member preference, which answers a different question from supplier quality.

questions.solution_text:
The $94\%$ cannot be checked: without a sample size it could rest on four clubs, and without knowing how the clubs were chosen there is no way to tell whether unhappy clubs were ever asked.
The report is not therefore worthless — it is incomplete, and the missing pieces are exactly what the committee needs.
**Ask the supplier how many clubs were asked and how they were chosen before deciding**.
